newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian minister sex charges seem thin - politicians.
newsitem.headline: Belgian minister sex charges seem thin - politicians.

text.p: Members of a Belgian parliament commission looking into allegations that Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo had sex with under-age boys said the case against him was thin.

"We are looking into the possibility of letting Mr. Di Rupo be heard by the court without going through the heavy procedure (of lifting his constitutional immunity)," commission member Albert Gehlen told reporters in parliament.
Gehlen is a member of the PSC, the francophone Christian-Democratic party which is one of the four parties in Belgium's centre left coalition.

"The allegations against Di Rupo are very thin and do not seem well-founded," federal Science Minister Ivan Ylieff, a francophone Socialist like Di Rupo, told reporters. Ylieff is not a member of the commission

Di Rupo, a colourful 45-year-old known for his bow-ties, does not deny being a homosexual but says he had sex only with consenting adults. Homosexuality is not a crime in Belgium. Sex with children younger than 16 is.

The commission must decide whether there is enough evidence in a report from the Brussels prosecutor- general to lift Di Rupo's immunity from prosecution and refer him to the Cour de Cassation, the highest court.
Political sources said the commission discussed the report and had heard the Brussels prosecutor-general this morning.
Di Rupo's spokesman, Bart Cammaerts, said the minister did not intend to appear before the commission. "Parliament has to make up its mind independently," he told Reuters.
Belgian daily De Morgen quoted the two Flemish socialist members of the commission as saying that the allegations against Di Rupo were not very substantial.
They said they favoured a solution whereby the court would be asked to come up with more facts before parliament could consider lifting Di Rupo's constitutional immunity.

Several Belgian papers said the 29-page report contained detailed allegations against Di Rupo dating back to the late 1980s from a man, arrested in connection with a child porn video case, who was 15 at the time.
Belgian radio said the 11 members of the panel would probably try to reach a decision on Wednesday.
Formally the commission, made up of parliamentarians from the main parties, puts a recommendation on the Di Rupo case to parliament, which then votes on it in a full session.
The procedure is similar to the one that brought down Belgian NATO Secretary General Willy Claes last year.
Parliament referred him to the Cour de Cassation over allegations of bribery in an army contract in the late 1980s. He has still not been tried.
Belgian law says that a minister can be questioned, confronted by witnesses or prosecuted, and his property searched, only once a full session of the lower house has voted to lift his immunity.
A date for a parliamentary vote on the commission's recommendation has not yet been set. A simple majority of the 150-seat house is needed to implement the commission's advice.
Parliament has three options when it comes to a vote.

It can adopt the prosecutor's request and bring Di Rupo before the Cour de Cassation, a move which would immediately end his political career. Parliament can also reject the court's request, which is unlikely.
But political sources said that the commission was increasingly looking at a so-called "third way", which would consist of allowing the court to hear Di Rupo, but without lifting his immunity.

The accusations against Di Rupo follow an unconnected scandal of paedophile abduction, sexual abuse and murder that has shaken Belgium to the core since the arrest of convicted rapist Marc Dutroux in mid-August.
